new_leaves.label: Masks of Burkina Faso
new_leaves.defn: The painted wooden masks of the Volta River peoples of Burkina Faso and southern Mali: the tall plank masks (nwantantay) and animal masks of the Bwa, the masks of the Bobo, Nuna, Winiama and other Gurunsi-speaking peoples, the Mossi karanga, and the Nafana bedu, covered with red, white and black geometric patterns and danced at funerals, initiations and agricultural festivals.
new_leaves.aliases: Voltaic masks; Bwa masks; Plank masks
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Masks+of+Burkina+Faso
The Met collection search: Masks of Burkina Faso
Masks of Burkina Faso in the Metropolitan Museum
new_leaves.axis: types, then the peoples who make it, then holding institutions
kinds: Bwa plank mask surmounting a disk-shaped face
Bwa masks of leaves dedicated to Dwo

new_leaves.label: Guro Masks
new_leaves.defn: The masks of the Guro (Kweni) of central Côte d'Ivoire: the sacred family of zamble, with its fused antelope and crocodile muzzle, his wife gu and his wild brother zauli, danced at funerals of lineage elders, and entertainment masks designed by individual performers; also heddle pulleys carved with heads.
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Guro+Masks
The Met collection search: Guro Masks
Guro Masks in the Metropolitan Museum
new_leaves.axis: types, then the peoples who make it, then holding institutions
kinds: female face mask, wife of zamble

new_leaves.label: Baga Headdresses
new_leaves.defn: The carved headdresses of the Baga of coastal Guinea: the colossal d'mba (nimba) shoulder mask of the great mother, the a-Mantsho-ña-Tshol serpent headdress, and the banda, danced at planting and harvest festivals, marriages and funerals; suppressed in the 1950s and revived since the 1980s.
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Baga+Headdresses
The Met collection search: Baga Headdresses
Baga Headdresses in the Metropolitan Museum
new_leaves.axis: types, then the peoples who make it, then holding institutions

new_leaves.label: Benue River Valley Sculpture
new_leaves.defn: The sculpture, masks and ceramic spirit vessels of the peoples of the Benue River valley in central Nigeria: Mumuye columnar figures and sukuru masks, Chamba buffalo masks, Jukun, Mambila, Tiv, Idoma and Igala figures and masks, Ga'anda and other Upper Benue spirit vessels, and the iron and bronze regalia of the region.
new_leaves.aliases: Arts of the Benue River Valley; Central Nigerian sculpture

new_leaves.label: Ekpo Masks
new_leaves.defn: The masks of the Ekpo men's society of the Ibibio and Anang of south-eastern Nigeria, worn at the festival after the yam harvest when the ancestors return: dark idiok ekpo masks of evil spirits and pale mfon ekpo masks of beauty, with Ibibio marionettes and ancestor figures.
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Ekpo+Masks

Ekpo Masks in the Metropolitan Museum
new_leaves.axis: types, then the peoples who make it, then holding institutions
kinds: dark mask of an evil spirit

new_leaves.label: Niger Delta Water-Spirit Masks
new_leaves.defn: The masquerade headdresses of the Niger Delta: horizontal Ijo and Kalabari crests of water spirits in the form of hippopotamus, sawfish, shark and crocodile, performed by the Ekine society, and the articulated-jaw masks of the Ogoni.
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Niger+Delta+Water-Spirit+Masks

Niger Delta Water-Spirit Masks in the Metropolitan Museum

new_leaves.label: Cross River Skin-Covered Headdresses
new_leaves.defn: The dance crests of the Ejagham, Boki and neighbouring peoples of the Cross River in Nigeria and Cameroon: heads carved in wood and covered with soaked antelope skin, often Janus-faced, with pegged teeth and coiffures, owned by age and entertainment associations and worn at funerals and initiations.

new_leaves.label: Urhobo Masks and Sculpture
new_leaves.defn: The masks and figures of the Urhobo of the western Niger Delta: water-spirit masks danced at festivals for spirits who travel upriver, the maiden masks with bridal coiffures, and the large edjo shrine figures.

new_leaves.label: Yaka and Suku Masks
new_leaves.defn: The masks of the Kwango-Kwilu region of the Democratic Republic of the Congo: the polychrome Yaka masks with upturned noses and raffia ruffs, held by a handle and danced in pairs at the close of the n-khanda boys' initiation, the Suku hemba helmet masks, and the masks of the Holo, Huana and Mbun.

new_leaves.label: Mbole Ofika Figures
new_leaves.defn: The ofika figures of the Mbole of the Lomami River region, Democratic Republic of the Congo: slender, hunched figures of hanged men, painted ochre and white, shown at the close of initiation into the Lilwa association to teach its law.

new_leaves.label: Kanak Sculpture
new_leaves.defn: The carving of the Kanak of New Caledonia: flèches faîtières (roof finials) and door jambs of the great clan houses, ancestor figures, masks of feathers and hair, and ceremonial axes and clubs.

new_leaves.label: Buka Ceremonial Paddles
new_leaves.defn: The carved and painted ceremonial paddles and dance clubs of Buka and Bougainville in the northern Solomon Islands, decorated in red, black and white with the kokorra, a squatting human figure wearing the upe headdress of male initiates.

new_leaves.label: Marshall Islands Stick Charts
new_leaves.defn: The navigational charts of the Marshall Islands: frames of palm-frond midribs bound with coconut fibre, curved sticks for ocean swells and cowrie shells for islands (mattang, meddo and rebbelib), used to teach voyaging and since the 20th century also made for sale.
catalogues: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search?q=Marshall+Islands+Stick+Charts

Marshall Islands Stick Charts in the Metropolitan Museum

kinds: chart of a whole island chain

new_leaves.label: Rai Stones
new_leaves.defn: The stone discs of Yap, quarried from aragonite on Palau and carried by canoe and raft, ranging from a few centimetres to several metres across, displayed outside houses and community buildings and exchanged at marriages, funerals and other ceremonies.

new_leaves.label: Palauan Storyboards
new_leaves.defn: The carved and painted narrative wood panels of Palau, derived from the carved beams and gables of the bai (men's clubhouse) and since the 1930s made as portable boards, telling legends such as the breadfruit tree and the Yapese currency quarrying.

new_leaves.label: Austral Islands Carving
new_leaves.defn: The woodcarving of the Austral Islands of French Polynesia: the deity figure A'a of Rurutu, the ceremonial paddles and ladles of Raivavae and Tubuai carved with interlocking geometric motifs and small human figures, fly whisks and drums.

new_leaves.label: Lenca Pottery
new_leaves.defn: The pottery of the Lenca of western Honduras and eastern El Salvador, made by hand by women from pre-Columbian times to the present: orange and brick-coloured household ware, and since the 1980s the black-and-white painted pottery of the La Campa and Gracias cooperatives.

new_leaves.label: Kadiwéu Ceramics
new_leaves.defn: The pottery of the Kadiwéu (Caduveo) of Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil: vessels, plates and figures painted with the minute symmetric scroll designs the Kadiwéu also paint on faces and bodies, recorded by Guido Boggiani and Claude Lévi-Strauss.

new_leaves.label: Selk'nam Body Painting
new_leaves.defn: The body painting of the Selk'nam (Ona) of Tierra del Fuego in red, white and black, with designs for hunting, combat and peace, and the totemic designs and bark masks of the spirits of the Hain initiation ceremony, photographed by Martin Gusinde in 1919–1924.

new_leaves.label: Quillango
new_leaves.defn: The painted guanaco-skin robes of the Tehuelche (Aónikenk) of Patagonia, sewn from many pelts, worn fur inward with the painted side out, decorated with red, black and yellow geometric designs.

new_leaves.label: Naskapi Painted Coats
new_leaves.defn: The painted caribou-skin coats of the Innu (Naskapi) of Quebec and Labrador, cut on the model of European frock coats and painted with dream-given designs in mineral and plant pigments bound with fish roe, with a triangular back gusset for the mountain of the Caribou Master; worn for one hunting season.

new_leaves.label: Huastec Sculpture
new_leaves.defn: The stone sculpture of the Huastec of the Gulf Coast of Mexico (c. 900–1521): sandstone figures of deities and rulers, naturalistic bodies with tall conical or fan headdresses, carved fully in the round in the Postclassic, with shell ornaments and effigy vessels.

new_leaves.label: Maroon Arts of Suriname
new_leaves.defn: The woodcarving, textiles and painting of the Saramaka, Ndyuka, Aluku and other Maroon peoples of Suriname and French Guiana: low-relief and openwork carved paddles, combs, stools and house fronts with tacks and inlays, appliqué and embroidered capes, and the painted carving of the eastern Maroons.

new_leaves.label: Pyu Architecture
new_leaves.defn: The brick architecture of the Pyu city-states of the Irrawaddy dry zone (2nd century BCE – 9th century CE): the walled and moated cities of Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra with palace citadels and the cylindrical memorial stupas of the earliest Buddhist urban culture in Southeast Asia; UNESCO World Heritage 2014.

new_leaves.label: Tangut Buddhist Painting
